audits.claim: Japanese: referent honorifics in three families — sonkeigo (raise the other), kenjōgo (lower self/group), teineigo (neutral-polite) — plus bikago "beautification" (Harada 1976; official taxonomy: Bunkachō 2007).
audits.entry_locator: §4 'Honorific systems, the deep end', Japanese bullet, line 84
audits.source_locator: Bunkachō (2007) 「敬語の指針」(文化審議会答申): 第1章「＜答申の立場＞（２）敬語の区分について」, printed p. 3; 第2章 第1「敬語の種類と働き」3「謙譲語Ⅱ」補足, printed p. 19; 4「丁寧語（「です・ます」型）」, printed p. 20. Excerpt is a composite; ellipses mark omitted text.
audits.source_excerpt: 本答申の第２章以降では，敬語を「尊敬語・謙譲語Ⅰ・謙譲語Ⅱ・丁寧語・美化語」の５種類に分けて解説する。… 「です」「ます」は＜相手＞に対する敬語として働く。… 謙譲語Ⅰは＜向かう先＞（相手側又は第三者）に対する敬語，謙譲語Ⅱは＜相手＞に対する敬語である。
audits.basis: The official taxonomy has five categories, not three-plus-bikago, and separates referent-directed honorifics (尊敬語, 謙譲語Ⅰ — directed at ＜向かう先＞ 'the target', the addressee-side or a third party) from addressee-directed ones (丁寧語 and 謙譲語Ⅱ/丁重語 — directed at ＜相手＞ 'the addressee'). Teineigo (desu/masu) is therefore the paradigm addressee honorific; grouping it under 'referent honorifics' conflates the addressee and referent axes that the entry itself needs to keep apart. The in-group/out-group (uchi/soto) point later in the bullet is unaffected. The cited Harada (1976) typology was not re-read; the correction rests on the retrieved official full text only. Recorded as erratum E1 in the entry.
audits.access_limit: Japanese-language full PDF retrieved and converted with pdftotext; no English edition consulted; printed page numbers are as they appear in this PDF; section titles verified against the retrieved table of contents.

audits.claim: Korean: separates addressee honorification (sentence-final speech levels — seven classical, four to six alive) from referent honorification (subject suffix -si-) (Lee & Ramsey 2000).
audits.source_locator: Ku, Jeong Yoon (2014), 'Korean Honorifics: A Case Study Analysis of Korean Speech Levels in Naturally Occurring Conversations', MA sub-thesis, Australian National University, §1.2.1 'Predicate Endings (Speech Levels, Hearer Honorifics)', p. 5
audits.source_excerpt: It is commonly divided into two main groups: hearer and referent honorifics (Yeon & Brown, 2011, p. 6). These honorifics … appear as speech levels (hearer honorifics) … as well as address/reference terms (Sohn, 1999, p. 16).
audits.basis: The retrieved ANU sub-thesis states the two-way hearer/referent partition and assigns speech levels to hearer (addressee) honorification, matching the entry's distinction; it adds that speech levels index the speaker's social relationship with participants. This audits the distinction only, not the level count (see SR-REG-04).
audits.access_limit: MA sub-thesis, not peer-reviewed; its attributions (Yeon & Brown 2011; Sohn 1999) were not independently re-read; Lee & Ramsey (2000), the entry's registered source, was not retrieved.

audits.claim: Referent honorification identified as the 'subject suffix -si-', separate from addressee honorification.
audits.source_locator: Kim, Yoolim & Findlay, Jamie Y. (2023), 'On the "subject" honorific -si- in Korean', Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 8(1): 5534, abstract and §1 (excerpt is a composite; ellipses mark omitted text)
audits.source_excerpt: This suffix has traditionally been described as a 'subject honorific' … It is well known, however, that this is an inadequate characterisation … the target of -si- is the human referent which is 'closest' to the subject.
audits.basis: -si- is referent-directed honorification in the entry's sense, but the retrieved paper documents that its target is settled pragmatically (the closest human referent), not syntactically as 'the subject'. It also records uses that honor the addressee, leading some to suggest that -si- is shifting towards being an addressee honorific (citing Kim-Renaud 2001). The entry's parenthetical '(subject suffix -si-)' is therefore a simplification, not an error; the addressee/referent labels are idealizations for Korean too.
audits.access_limit: Open-access proceedings paper; the cited Kim-Renaud (2001) was not retrieved; the retrieved text is peer-reviewed proceedings, not a handbook chapter.

audits.claim: Sentence-final speech levels: 'seven classical, four to six alive'.
audits.source_locator: Ku (2014), §1.2.1, p. 6 and Table 1.1 'Four Korean speech levels in frequent use today'
audits.source_excerpt: There are six speech levels indicated by sentence-final suffixes attached to verbs and adjectives (Table 1.1) (Sohn, 1999). Among these six, four are commonly in use in contemporary Korean society (Cho et al., 2010, p. 8).
audits.basis: The retrieved full text supports 'four alive' but gives six, not seven, for the fuller inventory; 'seven classical' is not attributed to any retrieved source and conflicts with this count. Traditions differ (some count 하소서체 as a level, others not), and the institutional check failed: www.korean.go.kr and stdict.korean.go.kr did not resolve from this environment (DNS timeout). Left explicitly unresolved; an Academy of Korean Studies encyclopedia search (encykorea.aks.ac.kr) also produced no retrievable article for the count; no marker was renamed or cleared.
audits.access_limit: One retrieved secondary full text plus failed institutional fetches; the National Institute of Korean Language's own count could not be checked on 2026-10-17. Treat both numbers as open.

audits.claim: Javanese: ngoko (plain) vs krama (polite) vs krama inggil (high honorific vocabulary) plus mixed madya; a sentence can be re-graded word-by-word to fine-tune relative status — status talk is live negotiation, not table lookup (Geertz 1972; Errington 1988).
audits.source_locator: Errington, Joseph (1982), 'Speech in the Royal Presence: Javanese Palace Language', Indonesia 34: 89–101 (Cornell Southeast Asia Program). Excerpt is a composite of three passages; ellipses mark omitted text; full text also retrieved from the eCommons bitstream.
audits.source_excerpt: This vocabulary marks a distinct way of speaking to people rather than of them; it defines a style of address, not reference. … both mark speaker's deference through linguistic reference.
audits.basis: The retrieved article distinguishes address-oriented honorific vocabulary from krama inggil-type deference 'through linguistic reference' — Javanese carries both an addressee-honorific and a referent-honorific resource, which is the distinction this recheck targets. Madya-adjacent usage lets politeness be raised or lowered element by element (in madya one may 'raise' or 'lower' politeness 'through choice of krama or ngoko elements'; matching 're-graded word by word'), and in royal audience usage was obligatorily symmetric krama for courtiers addressing one another regardless of office — register keyed to institution and occasion rather than a fixed status table, which is the rank/institution coupling tested here.
audits.access_limit: Article documents palace language (basa kedhaton) specifically, not all everyday Javanese; the entry's general claim rests on the cited Errington (1988) book, which was not re-read. The retrieved item is the 1982 article, not the 1988 monograph. OCR shows minor character errors (e.g., 'o f' for 'of'); normalized in the excerpt without changing sense.

audits.claim: Dyirbal speakers use guwal (everyday) in most contexts and switch wholly to jalnguy in the presence of taboo kin (Dixon 1980).
audits.source_locator: Australian Academy of the Humanities, 'The marvels of Indigenous language: edible gender & "mother-in-law" talk', October 2021, section 'A world of grammatical wonders', paragraph 4
audits.source_excerpt: it was taboo to directly address a mother-in-law, father-in-law, son-in-law or daughter-in-law. When talking within earshot of one of these relatives, a different speech style called Jalnguy – with a different vocabulary – was used.
audits.basis: Institutional source on Dixon's Dyirbal fieldwork confirms both elements: the trigger is the presence (earshot) of the taboo affines, not only direct address, and jalnguy is a distinct vocabulary. This couples the register to kinship taboo (language × kinship/ritual domain) rather than testing an isolated bibliography fact.
audits.access_limit: Academy outreach summary of Dixon's work, not the primary grammar; Dixon (1980) itself was not retrieved. The kin set named is specific to the source; no claim is made here about every Dyirbal avoidance context.

audits.source_locator: Haviland, John B., 'Guugu Yimithirr Brother-in-law Language' (chapter version; a version first appeared in Language in Society 8: 365–393), section on the structure of the BIL vocabulary
audits.source_excerpt: Like the Dyirbal Mother-in-law language (Dixon 1971), it may render a large number of ordinary EV words by a single BIL equivalent, using various circumlocutions.
audits.basis: The retrieved scholarly text describes avoidance lexicons — including, by its own citation of Dixon (1971), the Dyirbal mother-in-law language — as selective and many-to-one: one avoidance word can cover many ordinary words (presence-activation of such vocabulary is separately supported in SR-REG-06). So 'complete replacement lexicon' should not be read as one-to-one synonymy across the whole vocabulary. Whether jalnguy has an equivalent for every guwal lexeme (Dixon's own formulation) could not be confirmed from retrieved sources; retained unresolved as a scope caveat, not a refutation of the register's existence.
audits.access_limit: Secondary scholarly account with explicit attribution to Dixon (1971); Dixon (1971, 1980) were not retrieved. The primary target language of the retrieved article is Guugu Yimidhirr, with Dyirbal reached only through its citation.

audits.source_locator: Cambridge University Library, 'Greek diglossia and the language question through history and literature', 7 October 2019, paragraph on the post-junta period
audits.source_excerpt: Kathareuousa which had once been the official language of the government and judiciary documents, newspapers and technical publications, was now replaced with Demotiki as part of the 1976 Education Act.
audits.basis: Institutional library source confirms the 1976 date and the mechanism (an Education Act switching official and educational language to Demotic), i.e., the era × state-institution coupling behind the entry's '(settled 1976)'. A separate open-access education-history article retrieved this pass (Foukas 2018, Espacio, Tiempo y Educación 5(1): 71–93) discusses the 1976–1977 reform period but does not mention the language settlement, so it is not used as support.
audits.access_limit: Library blog post, not peer-reviewed; the statute itself (commonly cited as Law 309/1976) was not retrieved, so the legal number is deliberately not asserted here. The date 1976 is confirmed; wider claims about earlier or later stages of the Greek language question are outside this row.
